questions.sentence: I have lived in this city since five years.
answers: I have lived in this city for five years.
questions.explanation: Use "for" with a period of time and "since" with a starting point.

questions.sentence: I have seen that film last week.
answers: I saw that film last week.
questions.explanation: "Last week" is a finished time, so we need the past simple, not the present perfect.

questions.sentence: She is the more intelligent student in the class.
answers: She is the most intelligent student in the class.
questions.explanation: Use the superlative ("the most") when comparing one person with a whole group.

questions.sentence: My new flat is more bigger than my old one.
answers: My new flat is bigger than my old one.
questions.explanation: Short adjectives take -er. Never use "more" and -er together.

questions.sentence: This is the worse meal I've ever eaten.
answers: This is the worst meal I've ever eaten.
questions.explanation: The superlative of "bad" is "the worst"; "worse" is the comparative.

questions.sentence: I enjoy to go to the gym after work.
answers: I enjoy going to the gym after work.
questions.explanation: "Enjoy" is followed by the -ing form.

questions.sentence: I'm looking forward to see you on Saturday.
answers: I'm looking forward to seeing you on Saturday.
questions.explanation: In "look forward to", "to" is a preposition, so it is followed by -ing.

questions.sentence: She decided taking a yoga class.
answers: She decided to take a yoga class.
questions.explanation: "Decide" is followed by the infinitive with "to".

questions.sentence: Despite it was raining, we went for a run.
answers: Although it was raining, we went for a run.
Despite the rain, we went for a run.
Even though it was raining, we went for a run.
questions.explanation: "Despite" must be followed by a noun or -ing form, not a full clause.

questions.sentence: In spite of feel tired, he finished the race.
answers: In spite of feeling tired, he finished the race.
questions.explanation: After "in spite of", use the -ing form.

questions.sentence: The bridge was build in 1890.
answers: The bridge was built in 1890.
questions.explanation: The passive uses the past participle: build, built, built.

questions.sentence: The results will announced tomorrow.
answers: The results will be announced tomorrow.
questions.explanation: The future passive needs "be": will be + past participle.

questions.sentence: My bike has been stole.
answers: My bike has been stolen.
questions.explanation: The past participle of "steal" is "stolen".

questions.sentence: I am used to get up at six every day.
answers: I am used to getting up at six every day.
questions.explanation: "Be used to" is followed by the -ing form.

questions.sentence: When I was young, I use to play football every day.
answers: When I was young, I used to play football every day.
questions.explanation: In positive sentences, the form is "used to".

questions.sentence: Did you used to live in Seoul?
answers: Did you use to live in Seoul?
questions.explanation: After "did", write "use to" without -d.

questions.sentence: If it will rain tomorrow, we will stay at home.
answers: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.
questions.explanation: In the first conditional, use the present simple in the if-clause, not "will".

questions.sentence: If I would have more money, I would travel the world.
answers: If I had more money, I would travel the world.
questions.explanation: In the second conditional, use the past simple in the if-clause.

questions.sentence: If I was you, I would apologise.
answers: If I were you, I would apologise.
questions.explanation: The standard expression for advice is "If I were you".

questions.sentence: You should to talk to your teacher.
answers: You should talk to your teacher.
questions.explanation: "Should" is followed by the base form without "to".

questions.sentence: You had better to leave now.
answers: You had better leave now.
questions.explanation: "Had better" is followed by the base form without "to".

questions.sentence: She suggested me to join a study group.
answers: She suggested that I join a study group.
She suggested joining a study group.
She suggested that I should join a study group.
questions.explanation: "Suggest" is not followed by "someone + to + verb".

questions.sentence: Can you give me an advice?
answers: Can you give me some advice?
Can you give me a piece of advice?
Can you give me advice?
questions.explanation: "Advice" is uncountable, so it can't be used with "an".

questions.sentence: We need some informations about the tour.
answers: We need some information about the tour.
questions.explanation: "Information" is uncountable and has no plural form.

questions.sentence: How much suitcases are you taking?
answers: How many suitcases are you taking?
questions.explanation: Use "many" with plural countable nouns.

questions.sentence: There were less people at the beach than yesterday.
answers: There were fewer people at the beach than yesterday.
questions.explanation: Use "fewer" with countable nouns like "people".

questions.sentence: She is a engineer at a big company.
answers: She is an engineer at a big company.
questions.explanation: Use "an" before a vowel sound.

questions.sentence: I'd love to climb the Mount Everest one day.
answers: I'd love to climb Mount Everest one day.
questions.explanation: We don't use "the" with the names of single mountains.

questions.sentence: The life is too short to be unhappy.
answers: Life is too short to be unhappy.
questions.explanation: No article with uncountable nouns used in a general sense.

questions.sentence: When I arrived, the film already started.
answers: When I arrived, the film had already started.
questions.explanation: Use the past perfect for an action that happened before another past action.

questions.sentence: I was reading when the phone was ringing.
answers: I was reading when the phone rang.
questions.explanation: Use the past simple for the short action that interrupts a longer one.

questions.sentence: She was tired because she had been work all day.
answers: She was tired because she had been working all day.
questions.explanation: The past perfect continuous needs the -ing form: had been working.

questions.sentence: I'm very interested on wildlife documentaries.
answers: I'm very interested in wildlife documentaries.
questions.explanation: The correct preposition is "interested in".

questions.sentence: It depends of the weather.
answers: It depends on the weather.
questions.explanation: "Depend" is followed by "on".

questions.sentence: She is married with a biologist.
answers: She is married to a biologist.
questions.explanation: We say "married to" someone.

questions.sentence: The man which lives next door is a vet.
answers: The man who lives next door is a vet.
The man that lives next door is a vet.
questions.explanation: Use "who" or "that" for people, not "which".

questions.sentence: The tiger, that is endangered, lives in Asia.
answers: The tiger, which is endangered, lives in Asia.
questions.explanation: In a non-defining relative clause (with commas), use "which", not "that".

questions.sentence: That's the photographer who's pictures won the prize.
answers: That's the photographer whose pictures won the prize.
questions.explanation: "Whose" shows possession; "who's" means "who is".

questions.sentence: This is the park which we saw the deer.
answers: This is the park where we saw the deer.
This is the park in which we saw the deer.
questions.explanation: Use "where" (or "in which") for places when there's no object.

questions.sentence: I wish I can cook better.
answers: I wish I could cook better.
questions.explanation: "Wish" is followed by "could" (not "can") for abilities you don't have.

questions.sentence: I wish I didn't eat so much last night.
answers: I wish I hadn't eaten so much last night.
questions.explanation: For regrets about the past, use "wish + past perfect".

questions.sentence: If I had known, I would told you.
answers: If I had known, I would have told you.
questions.explanation: The third conditional result is "would have + past participle".

questions.sentence: If I would have studied, I would have passed.
answers: If I had studied, I would have passed.
questions.explanation: The third conditional if-clause uses the past perfect, not "would have".

questions.sentence: Could you lend your laptop me?
answers: Could you lend me your laptop?
Could you lend your laptop to me?
questions.explanation: Use person + thing, or thing + "to" + person.

questions.sentence: Can you explain me the problem?
answers: Can you explain the problem to me?
questions.explanation: "Explain" needs "to" before the person: explain something to someone.

questions.sentence: He must be at home. I just saw him at the gym.
answers: He can't be at home. I just saw him at the gym.
questions.explanation: For a negative deduction (it's impossible), use "can't", not "must".

questions.sentence: She mustn't be hungry. She's just eaten.
answers: She can't be hungry. She's just eaten.
questions.explanation: The opposite of "must" for deduction is "can't", not "mustn't".

questions.sentence: They must have went home already.
answers: They must have gone home already.
questions.explanation: "Must have" is followed by the past participle (gone).

questions.sentence: I will call you when I will arrive.
answers: I will call you when I arrive.
questions.explanation: After "when" referring to the future, use the present simple.

questions.sentence: This time tomorrow I will lie on the beach.
answers: This time tomorrow I will be lying on the beach.
questions.explanation: Use the future continuous for an action in progress at a future time.

questions.sentence: By next year, I will finish my degree.
answers: By next year, I will have finished my degree.
questions.explanation: Use the future perfect for an action completed before a future time.

questions.sentence: I had my hair cutted yesterday.
answers: I had my hair cut yesterday.
questions.explanation: "Cut" is irregular: cut, cut, cut.

questions.sentence: I need to get my car repair.
answers: I need to get my car repaired.
questions.explanation: Causative: get + object + past participle.

questions.sentence: The coach made us to run ten laps.
answers: The coach made us run ten laps.
questions.explanation: "Make someone do something" — no "to".

questions.sentence: The film was so bored that I fell asleep.
answers: The film was so boring that I fell asleep.
questions.explanation: Use "-ing" adjectives for the thing that causes the feeling.

questions.sentence: I was very interesting in the lecture.
answers: I was very interested in the lecture.
questions.explanation: Use "-ed" adjectives to describe how a person feels.

questions.sentence: She told that she was tired.
answers: She said that she was tired.
She told me that she was tired.
questions.explanation: "Tell" needs a person as an object; "say" doesn't.

questions.sentence: He asked me where did I live.
answers: He asked me where I lived.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use statement word order without "did".

questions.sentence: She said me that the story was true.
answers: She told me that the story was true.
She said that the story was true.
questions.explanation: Use "tell someone" or "say (to someone)", not "say someone".

questions.sentence: He denied to break the window.
answers: He denied breaking the window.
He denied having broken the window.
questions.explanation: "Deny" is followed by the -ing form.

questions.sentence: They accused him for stealing the money.
answers: They accused him of stealing the money.
questions.explanation: The correct pattern is "accuse someone of + -ing".

questions.sentence: She apologised for be late.
answers: She apologised for being late.
questions.explanation: After a preposition (for), use the -ing form.

questions.sentence: You don't have to smoke in the hospital. It's forbidden.
answers: You mustn't smoke in the hospital. It's forbidden.
You can't smoke in the hospital. It's forbidden.
questions.explanation: "Mustn't" means it's prohibited; "don't have to" means it's not necessary.

questions.sentence: We must to show our tickets at the entrance.
answers: We must show our tickets at the entrance.
questions.explanation: "Must" is followed by the base form without "to".

questions.sentence: My parents let me to go to the festival.
answers: My parents let me go to the festival.
questions.explanation: "Let someone do something" — no "to".

questions.sentence: After hours of searching, we could find the hotel.
answers: After hours of searching, we managed to find the hotel.
After hours of searching, we were able to find the hotel.
questions.explanation: For a single difficult achievement in the past, use "managed to" or "was able to".

questions.sentence: I'd love to can play the piano.
answers: I'd love to be able to play the piano.
questions.explanation: "Can" has no infinitive; use "be able to".

questions.sentence: She works like a shop assistant in Milan.
answers: She works as a shop assistant in Milan.
questions.explanation: Use "as" for someone's real job or role.

questions.sentence: He sings as a professional, but he's only a beginner.
answers: He sings like a professional, but he's only a beginner.
questions.explanation: Use "like" when comparing; he isn't really a professional.

questions.sentence: You needn't to bring anything to the party.
answers: You needn't bring anything to the party.
You don't need to bring anything to the party.
questions.explanation: "Needn't" is followed by the base form without "to".

questions.sentence: I should have study harder for the test.
answers: I should have studied harder for the test.
questions.explanation: "Should have" is followed by the past participle.

questions.sentence: What I need it is a long holiday.
answers: What I need is a long holiday.
questions.explanation: In a cleft sentence, "What I need is..." doesn't need "it".

questions.sentence: Never I have seen such a beautiful view.
answers: Never have I seen such a beautiful view.
questions.explanation: After "Never" at the start, invert the subject and auxiliary.

questions.sentence: Not only he was late, but he also forgot his CV.
answers: Not only was he late, but he also forgot his CV.
questions.explanation: After "Not only" at the start, invert the subject and verb.

questions.sentence: I felt very boring at the party.
answers: I felt very bored at the party.
questions.explanation: Use "-ed" adjectives for feelings.

questions.sentence: My sister and I get on very good.
answers: My sister and I get on very well.
questions.explanation: We need the adverb "well", not the adjective "good".

questions.sentence: I take after with my father.
answers: I take after my father.
questions.explanation: "Take after" doesn't need "with".

questions.sentence: I look up at my grandfather; he's my hero.
answers: I look up to my grandfather; he's my hero.
questions.explanation: "Look up to" means "admire".

questions.sentence: I have to resit the exam because I passed it.
answers: I have to resit the exam because I failed it.
questions.explanation: You resit an exam when you fail it.

questions.sentence: I lent a book from the library.
answers: I borrowed a book from the library.
questions.explanation: You "borrow" something from someone; you "lend" something to someone.

questions.sentence: Can you borrow me your pen?
answers: Can you lend me your pen?
questions.explanation: You "lend" something to another person.

questions.sentence: The new rules will effect everyone.
answers: The new rules will affect everyone.
questions.explanation: "Affect" is the verb; "effect" is usually a noun.

questions.sentence: These trousers are too lose.
answers: These trousers are too loose.
questions.explanation: "Loose" means not tight; "lose" means to stop having something.

questions.sentence: He gave me a good advise.
answers: He gave me some good advice.
He gave me good advice.
questions.explanation: "Advice" is the noun (uncountable); "advise" is the verb.

questions.sentence: I'm so full that I can't eat nothing else.
answers: I'm so full that I can't eat anything else.
questions.explanation: Avoid double negatives: use "anything" after a negative verb.

questions.sentence: The milk has went off.
answers: The milk has gone off.
questions.explanation: The past participle of "go" is "gone".

questions.sentence: I need to make a back up of my files.
answers: I need to make a backup of my files.
questions.explanation: The noun is written as one word: "backup".

questions.sentence: The wind is going to die off this afternoon.
answers: The wind is going to die down this afternoon.
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb for weather becoming less strong is "die down".

questions.sentence: This is by far the most hot day of the year.
answers: This is by far the hottest day of the year.
questions.explanation: "Hot" is a short adjective: the hottest.

questions.sentence: The spectaters cheered when he scored.
answers: The spectators cheered when he scored.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is "spectators".

questions.sentence: He made his debut in the national team on 2019.
answers: He made his debut in the national team in 2019.
questions.explanation: Use "in" with years.

questions.sentence: The journalist went to great length to find the truth.
answers: The journalist went to great lengths to find the truth.
questions.explanation: The fixed phrase is "go to great lengths".

questions.sentence: He finally came clear about his mistakes.
answers: He finally came clean about his mistakes.
questions.explanation: The idiom is "come clean" (tell the truth).

questions.sentence: The festival sold off in ten minutes.
answers: The festival sold out in ten minutes.
questions.explanation: "Sell out" means all the tickets have been sold.

questions.sentence: The price is a bit steeply for me.
answers: The price is a bit steep for me.
questions.explanation: "Steep" is an adjective here describing the price.

questions.sentence: She was promoted at manager last year.
answers: She was promoted to manager last year.
questions.explanation: We say "promoted to" a position.

questions.sentence: The company took over 50 new staff for the summer.
answers: The company took on 50 new staff for the summer.
questions.explanation: "Take on" means employ; "take over" means take control.

questions.sentence: Let's go over to the answers together.
answers: Let's go over the answers together.
questions.explanation: "Go over" (check carefully) is followed directly by the object.

questions.sentence: Please hand on your essays by Friday.
answers: Please hand in your essays by Friday.
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb is "hand in".

questions.sentence: I run into my old teacher yesterday.
answers: I ran into my old teacher yesterday.
questions.explanation: "Yesterday" needs the past simple: ran.

questions.sentence: She talked me in joining the choir.
answers: She talked me into joining the choir.
questions.explanation: The phrasal verb is "talk someone into + -ing".
